title: Allocation traps (hidden gen-0 storms)
hook: Not every allocation is obvious. String concatenation in a loop, LINQ that materializes lists, boxing a struct, and closure capture can flood generation 0 and pressure the garbage collector under Redis-heavy load.

blocks.text: Allocation traps are patterns that create more short-lived heap objects than you expect. Each new object costs a gen-0 slot. Closures capture locals into compiler-generated classes. Boxing wraps value types in heap objects. string + string in a loop allocates intermediate strings. LINQ operators like ToList() and ToArray() materialize entire sequences. Async state machines allocate a heap object per async method invocation.

entries.plainDefinition: Wrapping a value type in a heap object so it can be treated as object.
A hidden class that holds captured variables for a lambda.
entries.example: () => count++ captures count into a heap display class.

entries.plainDefinition: Forcing a deferred sequence into a concrete collection.
entries.example: .ToList() allocates a List and fills it.

blocks.text: A Redis cache service doing string concat per key lookup and LINQ ToList on every hit can allocate megabytes per second even when business logic is simple. Gen-0 collections are cheap individually, but allocation rate drives CPU spent in GC and causes gen-2 promotion for survivors. Fixing traps — StringBuilder, Span, deferred LINQ, struct alternatives — is often cheaper than buying more cores.

blocks.title: Measure first
blocks.body: Use dotnet-counters (System.Runtime) to watch allocation rate and GC heap size before micro-optimizing. Fix the hottest path shown in a trace.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Profile allocation rate
items.body: Watch alloc/sec under realistic Redis or HTTP load.

items.title: Inspect hot methods
items.body: dotnet-trace or a profiler shows which calls allocate.

items.title: Replace trap patterns
items.body: StringBuilder, TryFormat, IEnumerable without ToList, avoid boxing APIs.

items.title: Verify gen-0 pressure drops
items.body: Re-run counters; confirm fewer collections per request.

snippet.label: String concat trap vs StringBuilder
snippet.explanation: Each += creates a new immutable string. StringBuilder mutates an internal buffer with fewer allocations.

snippet.label: LINQ materialization trap
snippet.explanation: ToList() allocates a new List. Deferred execution is fine until you materialize on every request.

snippet.label: Closure and boxing
snippet.explanation: Each lambda may share one display class but still allocates. Boxing wraps the int in a heap object.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Calling ToList() or ToArray() inside tight loops. Using object or IComparable with structs. Logging with string interpolation on every cache hit at Debug level in production.

interviewTakeaways: Closures, boxing, string concat, and LINQ materialization are common gen-0 storms.
Prefer StringBuilder, deferred IEnumerable, and generic APIs over object.
commonPitfalls: ToList() on every Redis cache read.
Boxing value types through non-generic interfaces.
Assuming async adds zero heap allocations.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS also allocates on string concat and array methods. C# gives you Span and stackalloc to avoid some heap traffic — module 17.
